Wretched
rech'ed
adj. (miserable, afflicted, in a condition of distress; in Romans 7 the believer's honest cry under indwelling sin)
Old English wrecca, an exile or outcast, from the root that gives wreak — one driven out and miserable. The Greek in Romans 7:24 is talaiporos, worn down by hardship, wretched through toil and affliction.

Biblical Definition

“O wretched man that I am! who shall deliver me from the body of this death?” (Romans 7:24). The cry comes at the end of Paul's account of the war between the law of his mind and the law of sin in his members, and it is not despair — the very next verse answers it: “I thank God through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Romans 7:25). Wretchedness here is the mark of a living man. A corpse does not groan under corruption; only one who has been given a new nature can hate the old one. Moses had used the word of his own burden when he asked the LORD to kill him rather than let him see his wretchedness (Numbers 11:15). But the most terrible use is the one where the sufferer does not know: “Because thou sayest, I am rich, and increased with goods, and have need of nothing; and knowest not that thou art wretched, and miserable, and poor, and blind, and naked” (Revelation 3:17). Laodicea was wretched and comfortable. Paul was wretched and honest. The difference between them is the whole difference between a dead church and a living saint, and the counsel to Laodicea is to buy of Christ gold tried in the fire (Revelation 3:18) — that is, to become conscious of the poverty that was there all along.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines wretched as very miserable, sunk into deep affliction or distress, and also worthless or despicable.

expand to see more

WRETCHED, a. Very miserable; sunk into deep affliction or distress, either from want, anxiety or grief.

2. Calamitous; afflicting.

3. Very poor or mean; worthless; paltry.

4. Despicable; hatefully vile and contemptible.

MISERABLE, a. Very unhappy from grief, pain, calamity, poverty, apprehension of evil, or other cause.

Key Scripture

Romans 7:24 — "O wretched man that I am! who shall deliver me from the body of this death?"

Romans 7:25 — "I thank God through Jesus Christ our Lord. So then with the mind I myself serve the law of God; but with the flesh the law of sin."

Revelation 3:17 — "Because thou sayest, I am rich, and increased with goods, and have need of nothing; and knowest not that thou art wretched, and miserable, and poor, and blind, and naked:"

Numbers 11:15 — "And if thou deal thus with me, kill me, I pray thee, out of hand, if I have found favour in thy sight; and let me not see my wretchedness."

Modern Corruption

The cry of Romans 7 is medicalised into low self-esteem to be cured, when it is the groan of a regenerate man under remaining sin.

expand to see more

Therapeutic preaching hears O wretched man that I am and reaches for a remedy Paul never offers: a better estimate of the self. On that reading the verse describes a problem of self-perception, and the cure is to stop speaking of oneself in such terms. Paul's question is not how shall I feel better about myself but who shall deliver me from the body of this death, and the answer is a Person, not a reappraisal. The conviction is accurate. The man really is wretched in himself, and the deliverance really is outside him. Substituting self-regard for a Deliverer leaves the sin and removes the only cure.

The opposite error treats Romans 7 as a description of an unconverted man, or of a defective sort of Christian who has not yet reached a higher plane. The perfectionist strains of later revivalism made the chapter a stage to be graduated from. But the man speaking delights in the law of God after the inward man, serves it with his mind, and thanks God through Jesus Christ — none of which an unregenerate man does. The Reformed reading, held by the Puritans and written into the confessional doctrine of remaining corruption, takes the chapter as the normal experience of a believer who sees his own heart clearly. Laodicea is the warning at the other end: wretched, and unaware of it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek talaiporos (G5005), wretched through hardship — Romans 7:24, Revelation 3:17; Hebrew ra, evil or misery — Numbers 11:15.

expand to see more

Greek talaiporos (G5005) — wretched, worn down; only twice, Romans 7:24 and Revelation 3:17, and the two uses are opposites in self-knowledge.

Greek rhuomai (G4506) — to draw to oneself, to rescue; Romans 7:24, the deliverance Paul cries for.

Greek eleeinos (G1652) — pitiable, miserable; Revelation 3:17, joined to talaiporos in the verdict on Laodicea.

Hebrew ra — evil, distress; Numbers 11:15, Moses asking not to see his own wretchedness.

Romans 7:25 supplies the answer in the same breath as the cry: I thank God through Jesus Christ our Lord.

Usage

"“O wretched man that I am!” — the groan of a living saint, not a dying one."

"“Knowest not that thou art wretched” — Laodicea's wretchedness was the unfelt kind."

"Conviction of wretchedness is a mercy; the comfortable kind is the danger."
